content.text:
Sorcerer subclasses define your character thematically and often
	mechanically, and your subclass’s spells also greatly determine your play
	style. While any Sorcerer can fill any of the Sorcerer’s roles in the party by
	selecting appropriate spells, your subclass will provide you with options that
	might predispose you to one or more roles by giving you the tools to succeed
	with little further effort.

This article is for the 2024 DnD 5.5 rules. For the 2014 DnD 5e rules, see
	our
2014 DnD 5e Sorcerer Subclasses Guide
RPGBOT uses a color coding scheme which is simple to understand and easy to read at a glance. This system is designed to help players make informed decisions for their dnd character builds.

The Sorcerer’s psionics-adjacent, aberration-themed option, Aberrant Sorcery
	offers psychic abilities, a taste of Warlock spellcasting, and a little splash
	of body horror.

items.text:
: Consistently good almost
		all the way through.

: Mind Sliver is fantastic.
				Easily my favorite offensive cantrip.

: Arms of Hadar is passable as
				a panic option if you can’t cast Misty Step. Dissonant Whispers lets you
				force movement, allowing you to trigger Opportunity Attacks from your
				melee allies, and moving enemies away from you safely so that you never
				need to cast Arms of Hadar.

: Hunger of Hadar is an
				absolutely fantastic AOE damage and area control option. Sending is neat
				but only situationally useful.

: Evard’s Black Tentacles is a
				good spell, but it does less damage and has a smaller AOE than Hunger of
				Hadar, and also doesn’t scale with spell level, so there’s a lot of
				redundancy between the two. Summon Aberration is great, offering three
				very effective choices to suit your needs.

: Two excellent utility
				options. Rary’s Telepathic Bond feels like a weird choice since you get
				Telepathic Speech at first level, but Telepathic Speech is extremely
				limited so Rary’s Telepathic Bond is a big upgrade.

: A useful utility, but
		very limited compared to most forms of telepathy. You can communicate, but
		you still need to share a language, the duration is short, and you can only
		connect to one creature. That’s enough to send your party’s Scout off on
		their own with a way to remain in contact, but beyond stealth and subtlety
		there are few meaningful ways to use this.

: This saves you one or
		two Sorcery Points (depending on the spell level) when you spend Sorcery
		Points to get extra spell slots with Font of magic, you don’t need to spend
		the Bonus Action to convert Sorcery Points into spell slots, and you also
		get to cast the spell without verbal or somatic components (and some
		material components), so you get the benefits of Subtle Spell for free. If
		you’re getting a lot of use out of your subclass spells, this is very
		efficient.

: Psychic damage is rare,
		but charm and fear effects are very common.

: For a single Sorcery
		Point, every one of these effects is excellent. Replicating any of these is
		at least a 2nd-level spell, so the effects aren’t just good, they’re also
		cost-efficient. Note that since the fly and swim speeds are based on your
		walking speed, it’s easy to boost your new movement speed with buffs like
		Longstrider or Haste.

Personal note: Tyler finds the term “writhing sensory tendrils”
			upsetting.

: Great for setting up
		combos with Quicken Spell. Follow this with a quickened AOE damage spell
		like Meteor Swarm or area control spell like Force Cage and you can
		eliminate whole encounters in one turn even at this high level. The saving
		throw is Strength, though, and, with the exceptions of enemies who rely on
		magic in combat, many enemies will have high Strength saves.

content.text:
Where Wild Magic Sorcery is chaos, randomness, rerolls, and wacky fun chaos,
	Clockwork Sorcery is order, no rerolls, numerical minimums, and straight order
	and efficiency. It offers tools to solve a variety of problems in an orderly
	fashion, including spell options borrowed from the Cleric and Wizard. However,
	the Clockwork Soul leans heavily on its spell list, and the other subclass
	features are often only situationally useful, leaving the player to wait for
	these features to matter from time to time in between casting spells every
	turn.

items.text:
: Several excellent
		spells, including some cleric options like Aid and wizard options like
		Summon Construct and Wall of Force. Not everything on the list is a gem, of
		course.

: Protection from Evil and
				Good is a staple buff at any level, covering a wide range of dangerous
				creatures. Alarm is useful as a ritual.

: A staple utility option and
				an important defensive buff. Not glamorous or flashy, but hard to go
				without.

: Freedom of Movement is
				situationally useful, but helpful against enemies which like to grapple.
				Summon Construct is a Wizard exclusive, and it’s a decent summon option
				if you need a pet Defender.

: Greater Restoration isn’t as
				important as Lesser Restoration, but it’s still very important. The
				conditions which it fixes are miserable and in many cases borderline
				lethal. Wall of Force (another Wizard exclusive) is one of the best area
				control effects around, especially if you have another spellcaster in
				the party who can drop some ongoing area damage before you put your
				enemies inside the impenetrable hemisphere.

: This solves a lot of
		problems. Creatures which have Advantage on saves against specific
		conditions are common, and a Sorcerer encountering those resistances can
		hinder you a great deal. Similarly, if your allies have Disadvantage on a
		save (such as because they are Restrained or Poisoned), you can help protect
		them. The usage pool is limited, so save this for when it really
		matters.

: This is similar in many
		ways to Temporary Hit Points (though you can notably apply this on top of
		THP). The duration is great, and allowing the target to choose when to use
		the ward allows you to take a little damage when you know that there’s a
		Short Rest coming so that you can spend some Hit Point Dice to manage your
		limited resources.

Compare this to casting False Life. False Life is a 1st-level spell, so
			you can spend 2 Sorcery Points to get a spell slot with which to cast
			False Life. False Life lasts for grants 2d4+4 (average 9) THP. Each
			additional spell level adds 5 more THP. For those same 2 Sorcery points,
			you can give a creature a ward with 2 dice, which will prevent an average
			of 9 damage. Each additional Sorcery Points adds 4.5 more damage
			protection, compared to 1 or 2 Sorcery Points for 5 more temporary hit
			points from False Life. The two are roughly equivalent both in cost and
			effectiveness.

of DnD 5e
		assumes that players will succeed on attack rolls against a typical
		CR-appropriate AC if they roll an 8 or better (provided that your primary
		ability scores hits 16, 18, and 20 at levels 1, 4, and 8), giving players a
		65% chance of hitting an attack against an average, CR-appropriate enemy.
		Giving you a minimum guaranteed roll of 10 on attacks, saves, and ability
		checks means that you’re mostly guaranteed to hit with attacks, pass on any
		saves in which you’re proficient and have a decent ability score, and pass
		any ability checks with skills in which you’re well-suited. With a 1-minute
		duration, this is enough to get through one combat or to perform a series of
		skill checks if you move quickly.

This is a great ability on almost any other class, but on the Sorcerer
			its usefulness is extremely limited. Spells which require attack rolls
			(with the exception of cantrips) mostly vanished around 2nd-level spells
			unless you’re upcasting low-level spells like Scorching Ray. Sorcerers are
			proficient with Constitution saves so this helps with Concentration, so
			this helps a lot with that. Since Sorcerers are Charisma-based, most of
			your skills will be, too, and using Persuasion in combat doesn’t work
			particularly well. So the three best uses for this are cantrips, upcasting
			low-level spells like Scorching Ray, and Concentration. That’s
			underwhelming for an ability which costs 5 Sorcery Points to recharge.

: Even with three
		effects, this is still only situationally useful.

: The 100 points of healing will
				be the most consistently useful option for adventurers, allowing you to
				get allies back on their feet and restore a nice chunk of hit points.
				But at this level, healing options like Mass Cure Wounds and Heal have
				been around for a while, and Clerics are casting Mass Heal to do the
				same thing with a pool of 700 points.

: Neat, but rarely useful. This
				could be used to solve some puzzles, though: Picture the

. Now picture the Rosetta Stone after a Clockwork Soul snaps their
				fingers and all the broken pieces that have been missing for millennia
				just reappear in place with complete text and all the wear and tear of
				time is undone.

: This outright ends spell
				effects without the ability checks required by Dispel Magic. But even
				then, it’s rare that you’ll face more than a small handful of enemies
				with magic effects on them, so in most cases you can just upcast Dispel
				Magic to level 6 to get the same effect if you don’t want to risk making
				the ability checks.

content.text:
The iconic Sorcerer, Draconic Sorcery perfectly complements the core of the
	class, providing tools to close gaps in the Sorcerer’s defenses and staple
	spells to address a wide variety of challenges. Elemental Affinity predisposes
	the Draconic Sorcerer to playing a blaster focused on a single element, but
	otherwise they enjoy the full breadth of the Sorcerer’s capabilities. You
	won’t excel in any one role compared to other Sorcerers, but Draconic Sorcery
	is hard to beat as a generalist.
DnD 5.5 Draconic Sorcery Sorcerer Subclass Guide

items.text:
: A fantastic
		improvement to your durability. Don’t go diving into melee, though.

: Almost everything on the
		spell list will be consistently useful, and many of the options are staple
		Sorcerer choices that I would recommend taking if they weren’t already on
		your subclass spell list.

: Command is a powerful crowd
				control option at any level. Chromatic Orb is good single-target
				damage.

: Alter Self is only
				situationally useful, but Dragon’s Breath can be a very efficient AOE
				damage option, especially if you cast it on a familiar that normally
				can’t do damage.

: A powerful crowd control
				option and a crucial utility.

: Arcane Eye is my favorite
				scouting option. Charm Monster is only situationally useful.

: Legend Lore is only useful
				if your DM feels like conducting a lore dump. Summon Dragon is great.

: Powerful, but the
		choice is definitely stressful. If you pick a more common damage type like
		Fire, you’ll get more use offensively, but you’ll run into resistances more
		often. If you pick a less common damage type like Lightning, you’ll have very
		few spell options, but damage resistances will be less of an issue. Don’t
		pick poison. It’s commonly resisted and there are few good spells that deal
		poison damage.

: As powerful and effective as
		casting Fly on yourself, but it doesn’t require Concentration.

: Summon Dragon is a level 5 spell, and at
		level 18 when you have level 9 spell slots, a level 5 summon spell isn’t
		especially impressive unless you upcast it. The free summoning won’t be
		especially impressive in combat, but since you’re not using a spell slot, you
		can cast another spell with a spell slot on the same turn, such as casting
		Misty Step as a Bonus Action.

Casting Summon Dragon without Concentration leaves room for you to do a lot
			of other cool stuff at the same time. Even if you’re repeatedly casting
			low-level versions of Summon Dragon as canon fodder, it can be a huge
			tactical advantage simply by flooding the battlefield with bodies for a
			few turns and wearing down enemies with the dragons’ breath weapons.

content.text:
Powerful and versatile with a good mix of features, the Shadow Sorcery
	Sorcerer is at its best in the dark. Even in areas of bright light, the
	magical darkness rules will give you a massive tactical advantage nearly any
	enemy.

Hound of Ill Omen makes the Shadow Magic Sorcerer an ideal save-or-suck
	caster, providing an easy and relatively inexpensive way to impose
	Disadvantage on targets’ saving throws. While your spell selection isn’t so
	broad as subclasses like Aberrant Mind and Clockwork Soul, the sheer
	incredible power of Hound of Ill Omen allows you to thrive with a very small
	spell selection.

items.text:
: You’ll get little value out
				of either spell. Bane may be helpful for burning through Legendary
				Resistances at low cost, but it’s hard to justify concentrating on it
				when you get so much our of casting Darkness.

: Darkness will be a go-to
				spell for you in many situations, but Pass Without Trace is harder for
				enemies to notice than a roving ball of darkness.

: Hunger of Hadar is one of the
				best area control spells available for a long time. Nondetection is only
				situationally useful, but its long duration may be worthwhile.

: Greater Invisibility is
				amazing, but you can usually get the same value by casting Darkness sine
				you can see through it. Phantamal Killer is a good offensive option,
				especially if you can debuff the target’s saves to keep the effect
				going.

: Both options are only
				situationally useful.

: 120 feet or
				Darkvision and the ability to see in magical darkness are already
				excellent, but adding Blindsight is just incredible.

: This could
				easily save your life, but it does get less reliable as damage scales
				and the DC increases. But at low levels, this is fantastic.

: A wildly powerful
		summon option, but you need to know what you’re getting. You don’t get
		Summon Beast prepared; this is a whole separate thing. You can’t treat this
		like a normal summon, either, because it isn’t one.

You activate Beasts of Ill Omen as a Bonus Action. No spell slot, no
			material components. You still pick the form of the beast, which gives you
			some flexibility, but the Air form is the right answer any time that
			you’re not underwater. While you are summoning a combat pet, the primary
			function of the pet is imposing Disadvantage on enemies’ saves. The Air
			form has Flyby, allowing it to fly in and out of reach without provoking
			Opportunity Attacks.

Unfortunately, the timing of the beast’s turn presents a problem: it acts
			immediately after you, which means that it may not be in position to
			impose Disadvantage when you want to cast a spell. You can Ready a spell
			to cast it once your beast is in position, but readying a spell takes
			Concentration, which can be a huge problem. You may be able to have your
			beast Ready an action to move before your next turn, but that’s a lot of
			setup with a lot of room for something to go wrong.

There isn’t an easy answer here unless enemies are happy to stay in melee
			with your best (or being forced to do so). Also, your beast’s hit points
			won’t scale because you’re casting Summon Beast without a spell slot, so
			you’re riding on AC and hope. Having your beast Dodge will help a lot.

Finally, when cast Summon Beast (normally or with this feature) you can
			choose to remove the Concentration requirement by dropping the duration to
			1 minute. The text specifies that this version of the spell ends early if
			you cast Summon Beast again, but nothing prevents you from casting it
			normally

: Free teleportation as a Bonus
		Action! The range is pretty good, and in a pinch you can cast Darkness to
		create an area in which to teleport. You can even use this while travelling,
		allowing you to move roughly 5 times as fast as normal by combining a
		comfortable walking pace and frequent teleportation.

: Once per Long Rest unless
		you spend a big pile of Sorcery Points, and you need to activate Innate
		Sorcery to activate this. It only lasts one minute, and the buffs are
		primarily defensive, so you don’t need to rush to use this in every fight,
		but it’s great for boss fights or when you expect to draw a lot of
		attention.

: Extremely
				powerful both in and out of combat. Unfortunately, Umbral Form only
				lasts 1 minute at a time.

: Resistance to
				nearly all damage. You can pick up immunity to Radiant damage from Boon
				of Blazing Dawn.

content.text:
Spellfire Sorcery borrows several spells from the Cleric and adds options
	which encourage you to use Counterspell. It’s an interesting mix of defenses
	and support, but the offesive options are so weak that they might as well not
	exist.

Given the choice, play Divine Soul instead. All of the healing and Radiant
	damage, plus the rest of the subclass fearures are better. Spellfire Sorcery
	isn’t awful, but it can’t compete with mechanically similar options that more
	powerful.

items.text:
: Two rider effects when you cast spells
		and spen Sorcery Points.

: A decent amount of
				Temporary Hit Points that you get to grant when you do stuff that you
				were going to do anyway.

: 1d4 damage. It scales up
				to 1d8 at level 14, but this is a pointless amount of damage.

: Mostly spells from
		the Cleric’s spell list. You get healing and condition removal, which is
		enough htat you could replace a Cleric in your party.

: You don’t get Healing
				Word, but you stil get good healing, and Guiding Bolt is a good go-to
				offensive option at low levels.

: Essential condition
				removal and a good damage option.

: Extend Spell on Aura
				of Vitality is a very efficient way to get a ton of healing for your
				party without resorting to resting. Dispel Magic is only situationally
				useful, but essential in any party.

: Wall of Fire is
				excellent area control.

: Greater Restoration
				is essential, but only situationally useful. Flame Strike is only useful
				if you can’t get Fireball.

: If you’re not fighting
		enemy spellcasters, this feature it outright useless. Even if you are
		fighting enemy spellcasters, you get very few Sorcery Points out of
		this.

: A ton of additional
		Temporary Hit Points, but the damage increase on Radiant Fire is insultingly
		poor.

: Flight and Spell
		Avoidance are great defensively. Crown of Spellfire is useful, but only if
		you have Hit Point Dice to power it. If you take a few hits over multiple
		turns, you could easily burn through all of your dice, at which points Crown
		of Spellfire is significantly less useful.

: An inefficient
				use of your Hit Point Dice, but prevention is better than healing, so it
				may make sense to use this instead of waiting to heal during a Short
				Rest.

content.text:
Whimsical and fun, but not especially powerful, Wild Magic has some great
	features, but the inherent unpredictability of Wild Magic makes it unreliable.
	Wild Magic Sorcery is also the only Sorcerer subclass in the 2024 PHB that
	does not have a spell list. Instead, you get Wild Magic. This is not a fair
	trade, and lacking the versatility provided by 10 additional prepared spells
	is a huge limitation compared to any other subclass.

Players coming from the 2014 rules should note that the Wild Magic effects
	table has changed significantly. Among other changes, the option to cast
	Fireball no longer forces you to center it on yourself.
Wild Magic Sorcerer Subclass Guide

items.text:
: A 1 in 20 chance to roll on
		the Wild Magic table isn’t significant. You don’t get 20 spell slots until
		you’re level 19, which means that you’re likely to go days at a time without
		triggering Wild Magic this way even if you try your hardest to do so. Instead, expect to trigger surges by using Tides of Chaos.

The effects of Wild Magic are mostly benign, but there are a few options
			like Polymorphing yourself into a goat or casting Fireball on your party.
			But, since those options are in the minority, Wild Magic is usually
			safe and frequently helpful, though the unpredictable effects mean that
			you can’t count on it to be consistently useful.

: Use this on any ability
		check or saving throw where the outcome matters more than a handful of hit
		points. Easy Advantage that you can recharge this easily is incredibly
		powerful.

If you’re not expecting many fights on any given day, you can use level 1
			spell slots to easily recharge this, then inexpensively replenish the
			slots with Font of Magic. This can be fantastic for social situations and
			for exploration, though Enhance Ability will be less expensive for
			numerous ability checks of the same type in quick succession.

: When your allies fail a save
		against death by 1 or two, it’s heart-breaking. Spend the Sorcery Points and
		be everyone’s best friend. 2 Sorcery Points is expensive, but your allies’
		lives are worth it.

Conversely, if an enemy narrowly passes a save against a level 1+,
			spending 2 Sorcery Points to turn that into a failure is absolutely worth
			the cost. 2 Sorcery Points could get you a level 1 spell slot, but it will
			never recover the Action you spent to cast a spell unsuccessfully.

: This considerably
		reduces the threat of the Wild Magic table and makes it more of a source of
		unpredictable buffs and comic relief.

: Many of the Wild Magic
		effects can be very beneficial if you can predict when they’ll occur. For
		example: Misty Step behind your enemies, make all creatures within 30 feet
		vulnerable to Piercing damage, then Dash and fly to safety. Unfortunately,
		you only get this once per Long Rest with no way to recharge it early.

sections.heading: Legacy Sorcerer Subclasses: DnD 5e Subclasses in the DnD 5.5 Rules

content.text:
Not all of the subclasses have been updated to the DnD 5.5 rules. The
	assessments below reflect the existing versions of the subclasses when used
	with the DnD 5.5 versions of the base class.

The 2024 rules were mostly buffs to the Sorcerer, giving them more spells
	known (sorry, “prepared”) and the new Innate Sorcery feature. Subclasses also
	consistently provide a subclass spell list now (excluding Wild Magic), so
	legacy subclasses which don’t have one have fallen behind a bit. Even so, the
	additional prepared spells are likely enough to keep them relevant. The
	changes to Ritual casting also allow the Sorcerer to cast Ritual spells,
	allowing you some utility without dipping into your spell slots.

If you can’t decide between playing a divine caster or an arcane caster, play
	a Divine Soul. Access to the Cleric’s spell list allows you to combine some of
	the best spell options in the game, allowing a single character to solve
	nearly any problem that can be solved using magic.

Divine Soul’s biggest challenge is the inherent analysis paralysis imposed by
	fitting two spell lists into your limited number of spells known. You simply
	can’t learn everything that you want to learn on one character. But that’s the
	guiding principle of the Sorcerer: you need to pick your favorites and use
	Metamagic to make those options work. And in the 2024 dnD 5.5 rules, the
	Sorcerer’s maximum number of spells known increased from 15 to 22, so you have
	much more flexibility.

items.text:
: Access to the Cleric spell
		list is amazing. They have many of the absolute best divine spells,
		including most of the best healing options, a ton of great support options,
		and many fantastic divinations. Unfortunately, you’ll need to split your
		focus between normal Sorcerer spells and pretending to be a Cleric, but the
		possibilities for combinations are amazing.

You also gain an additional spell known at level 1 based on your
			alignment. One spell doesn’t sound like a lot, but it’s still very useful
			for the Sorcerer.

: Important in most parties, but
				Healing Word is more frequently useful. The ability to cast it as Bonus
				Action with Quickened Spell may make this appealing, but remember that
				the range is Touch.

: The damage is poor beyond low
				levels, the scaling is bad compared to many Sorcerer spells, and getting
				into melee to use this is risky.

: A fantastic buff at any
				level.

: Decent but difficult to rely
				upon, and if you’re going to force Charisma saves you really want
				failure to be more meaningful than a small debuff. Still, Bane is a good
				way to burn through Legendary Resistances.

: Most features like
		this only grant 1d4 or 1d6, so 2d4 is excellent. This also recharges on a
		Short Rest, making it a frequent and reliable defensive option.

: The problem with this
		ability is the problem with healing in combat. If you’re in a fight, healing
		is rarely the best option. Death is easy to prevent in 5e, and if you’ve got
		Healing Word, you can get an ally back into the fight as a Bonus Action.

Being massively injured isn’t much of an impediment, so allies can limp
			around at 1 hp and still be perfectly effective. With the exception of
			Heal and a few other time-efficient healing options, getting a creature
			back to full hit points should generally be reserved for healing out of
			combat. Once you’re out of combat and your action economy isn’t limited,
			you usually don’t need to expend limited spell slots to scrape together
			every last hit point. Sit down and spend some hit dice.

But the 2024 DnD 5.5 rules also doubled the number of dice healed by
			Healing Word and Cure Wounds, so you’re getting twice as much value out of
			this as you did in the 2014 DnD 5e rules. Rerolling 4 and below on a d8
			increases the average from 4.5 to 5.5, which doesn’t feel like a lot, but
			will feel a lot better when you reroll a bunch of 1’s and 2’s. You don’t
			want to use this every time you heal someone, but sometimes it makes sense
			to go a bit further than a level 1 Healing Word just to get someone
			conscious.

: Persistent flight
		without Concentration is amazing at any level. There’s no usage limitation,
		either, so you can refresh this any time that you have a Bonus Action free.
		If they’re generous (or at least tolerant of your nonsense), your DM might
		let you activate this repeatedly outside of combat so that you always go
		into combat with your wings in effect.

: This could be a lot
		of healing, but by this level you probably know Heal, so your healing
		options are abundant. Of course, this doesn’t consume a spell slot, so you
		can use this and cast a spell with a spell slot at the same time.

content.text:
The Moon Mage from Planet Krynn. Lunar Sorcery comes to us from the
	Dragonlance campaign setting with some very strong features. Access to 15
	additional Prepared spells per day can offer some great versatility, even when
	compared to subclasses that get a subclass spell list, but comes at the cost
	of locking into one batch of 5 spells at any given time.

Lunar Sorcery can lean heavily both on your Bonus Action and on your Sorcery
	Points, which can be challenging, but offers flexibility for that cost. In the
	2024 DnD 5.5 rules, the Sorcerer’s expanded number of Prepared spells and
	every subclass providing additional prepared spells does make Lunar Sorcery
	less of a standout.

items.text:
: There are two halves to
		this feature. One half grants the Sorcerer 15 total spells known from a
		fixed list. The list is generally good.

The second half allows the user to cast one of the level spells once per
			day without expending a spell slot, depending on which Moon Phase is
			chosen at the start of the day. At higher levels, this expands to allow
			each of the three level 1 spells once each per day without expending a
			spell slot.

And by which phase you choose, we mean always Full Moon and only Full
			Moon from levels 3 through 5 where the only thing the phase controls is
			the free level 1. Because Full Moon is the Shield spell and the other two
			spells are too situational to need a free cast each day.

: One great spell, one okay
				spell, and one not great spell. All three are already on the Sorcerer
				list as well. Still, the good spell is something most Sorcerers already
				take so having it be available as a once per day free spell is even
				better.

: Fantastic options here. One
				great spell not on the Sorcerer list, and two spells ranked Green on our
				5.5 Sorcerer Spells Guide.

: Overall rather solid. Two
				spells from outside the Sorcerer list as well as a commonly taken spell
				for Sorcerers. While one of these spells is a bit niche, ranked Orange
				on the Wizard list even it still has occasional uses.

: One dud spell ranked red on
				the Sorcerer list is made up for by getting both a good and an okay
				spell from outside the Sorcerer list.

: Continuing the trend, one
				spell from the Sorcerer list, ranked blue this time, as well as two
				spells from outside the list. A very good blue ranked Wizard-only spell
				and a niche but still useful orange spell from Wizard.

: An additional Cantrip known
		that is normally exclusive to Cleric, but with a twist that allows it to hit
		an extra target. Strong boost when you can hit the extra target, but also
		nice to gain another out of class spell in a valuable damage type that’s
		hard to access.

If you take the Spellfire Spark Origin Feat, you can also cast Sacred
			Flame as a Bonus Action a few times per day, and that casting still
			benefits from Moon Fire. If you catch two enemies adjacent to each other,
			you could hit each of them with Sacred Flame twice in one turn without
			dipping into your Sorcery Points.

: An upgrade to Metamagic to
		really stretch out your Sorcery Points, as long as you prepare ahead of time
		for the schools of magic you want to add Metamagic to. Yes, because it can
		only be used PB times per Long Rest, it’s at most 6 more Spell Points worth
		of Metamagic at the high end, but that’s still more than other Sorcerers.

Remember that spells may have changed school of magic in the transition
			from 2014 5e to 2025 5.5. Healing spell are now Abjuration spells. Lunar
			Boons also doesn’t specify that it needs to affect Sorcerer Spells, so
			spells you get from other sources like Magic Initiate can still be
			affected.

: This is the feature
		that allows you to switch up your Moon Phase, changing, among other things,
		which schools of magic the enhancement to Metamagic from Lunar Boons is
		applied to. This also allows you to get the extra free level 1 spell from
		Lunar Embodiment, as discussed above.

Switching moon phases can be very useful, but keep an eye on the Sorcery
			Point cost.

: Three passive benefits
		depending on which Moon Phase we’re in.

: Being a flashlight with
				some extra benefits to searching for stuff is likely to be useful more
				often than not.

: Sneaky stealth mode for
				sneaky stealth missions. Imposing Disadvantage on attacks is only an
				improvement when fighting creatures that can see in darkness; everything
				else already has Disadvantage because you’re Heavily Obscured to
				them.

: Resistance to multiple
				uncommon damage types. Very useful at high levels as those damage type
				become more common.

: Three potent options
		that can each be used as a Bonus Action once per Long Rest, or repeated for
		5 Sorcery Points. As a great QoL feature, this can also be activated with
		the same Bonus Action that changes your form via Waxing and Waning. Meaning
		you could start in Full Moon, use Waxing and Waning to spend one Sorcery
		Point to switch to Crescent Moon and simultaneously activate the Crescent
		Moon Lunar Phenomenon.

: An AoE Con save to inflict
				Blindness for a round along with some minor healing, which is very nice
				but still the “weakest” of the three options.

: AoE damage and speed
				reduction paired with self Invisibility for a round as a non-spell Bonus
				Action, so you can still cast a spell as your Action.

: Short range
				teleportation and Resistance to all damage for you and a friend. Great
				for getting out of dangerous positions (or diving into them if you’re
				feeling adventurous).

content.text:
Storm Sorcery faces several issues, which is unfortunate because the flavor
	is really fun. Tempestuous Magic doesn’t scale, and in some ways it’s obsolete
	right when you get it thanks to Misty Step. The premise of the subclass
	requires you to stay just outside of melee range, dodging in to use Heart of
	the Storm before retreating with Tempestuous Magic, but on their own they’re
	not impactful enough to make that a good idea.

It’s an interesting premise, but it’s extremely risky. Unless you’re somehow
	boosting your speed (spells like Longstrider can help) or flying (aarakocra,
	owlin, etc.), you’re stuck within walking distance on your enemies’ turns.
	It’s much safer for Sorcerers to remain at the longest distance possible and
	assail their enemies from well outside of weapon range.

On top of the simple challenge of positioning, Heart of the Storm expects
	that you will know some spells which deal thunder or lightning damage, but you
	don’t get any for free. A misguided player could select spells which make
	Heart of the Storm totally useless. The selection of level spells which deal
	Lighting or Thunder damage isn’t huge, either, so your options are limited.

The introduction of Cacophonic Shield in Heroes of Faerun may be the best
	thing that has ever happened to the Storm Sorcerer. It works similarly to
	Spirit Guardians, but it’s a Con save, Thunder damage, and the debuff isn’t as
	impactful. So it’s worse than Spirit Guardians, but Sorcerers can learn it and
	it triggers Storm Sorcery’s features. If you have good speed or you can fly,
	turning yourself into a roving ball of Thunder damage can be decently
	effective.

items.text:
: Essentially four free
		languages. Especially nice if you are your party’s Face, but you can also
		cast spells to overcome language barriers.

: 10 feet of flight
		won’t get you anywhere interesting. The primary function is to remove you
		from melee combat without drawing Opportunity Attacks. But you can also cast
		Misty Step.

The fact that it’s free (once you’ve cast a spell with a spell slot) is
			nice, especially if you like to run into close quarters to deliver spells
			like Thunder Wave. If this worked with Cantrips, it would be a defining
			feature of the subclass, but limiting it to leveled spells makes this a
			situational novelty.

If you need a low-level way to trigger this, Chromatic Orb is an easy
			choice. Once you can cast Cacophonic Shield, this makes it easy to dive
			into crowds to damage everything in an encounter, then fly safely out of
			melee.

: Being within 10 feet
		of foes is rarely a good idea for a Sorcerer. The resistances are great, but
		it’s hard to bring the bonus damage into play without seriously endangering
		yourself.

Cacophonic Shield (which you’re now high enough level to cast) is a great
			combination here. Run into a crowd, cast Cacophonic Shield, have your
			enemies takes the guaranteed damage from Heart of the Storm, then use
			Tempestuous Magic to fly out of melee. Ideally, you want to move far
			enough that none of your enemies are inside the AOE of Cacophonic Shield
			so that they’re forced to take damage if they move toward you.
			Unfortunately, Heart of the Storm’s 10-foot radius may make that hard
			unless you have unusually high speed. Once Cacophonic Shield is in place,
			you can continue to trigger Heart of the Storm by casting Chromatic Orb,
			Shatter, or Thunder Step.

If you’re dragged into melee, you can also trigger this by transmuting
			Hellish Rebuke to deal Lightning or Thunder damage.

: Unless you’re in a seafaring
		campaign, this will almost certainly never matter.

: Great if enemies decided to
		chase you around. If you’re running Cacophonic Shield, this pushes them
		almost all the way out of the AOE, so you can walk a few feet away on your
		turn, then walk the Emanation back onto them to trigger the damage
		again.

: Permanent flight with an
		unusually good speed and withou Concentration. If you’re leaning into
		Cacophonic Shield, this makes your life much easier because you can move the
		full radius of the Emanation twice in one turn without needing additional
		movement speed.

You can also share the flight with your party for an hour each day,
			allowing you to get through several fights or travel short distances
			quickly. It’s not amazing for overland travel, but it’ll get your party
			over obstacles.
